en: The Kaṭhināvadāna.
Oṃ, homage to the Triple Gem!
His feet are worshipped by the multitude of sages; he has destroyed all defects and possesses supreme glory.
Victorious is the Jina, skilled in the welfare of the entire world, whose pure awakening is supreme;

he who is glorious, whose lotus feet are incessantly worshipped by gods and asuras alike, the manifest treasury of merit, the great preceptor of auspiciousness, the wish-fulfilling gem, the omniscient one.

May the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, the Jina Śauddhodani—whose tangle of the net of faults has been entirely uprooted, who has reached the further shore, and who blazes with radiant splendor—protect you all.
Immediately following this avadāna, he states the introductory narrative (*nidāna*):
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing [the answer] even while [inquiring] for the sake of others, addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"Blessed One, when does the *kaṭhina* robe arise?"
The Blessed One said: "Starting from the first day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, during the thirty days, on whichever day and night the kaṭhina robe-material for the Saṅgha arises,
that must be caused to be brought forth together with its accompanying garment."
Once the dyeing with the prepared lac has been completed according to the manual for blue thread, needle, and tools, those patrons should be made to remove it when the Saṃgha has assembled.
Then, a monk acting as the *karmakāraka* (executor of the formal act) should greet those patrons with a discourse on the preparation of the gift,
beginning with the words, "It is well-prepared," and so forth.

A donor who wishes to perform the bestowal of the *kaṭhina* should approach the noble Saṅgha with humility during the sixth or seventh month and make a formal request through the mouth of the *kalpika-kāraka*. He should do so as follows:
"Pay heed, noble Saṅgha! This person named so-and-so will spread the *kaṭhina*."
"If the noble Saṃgha accepts this, let it not otherwise; if not, let them forbid it.
Then, if the intention of the donor is pure and the object to be given is perfectly pure, he should accept it by remaining silent; if not, he should forbid it.
If the noble Saṃgha then gives its consent, one should dye a pair of well-measured, beautiful garments and show them to him.
Then the officer in charge of formal procedures, having taken that [material] and dismissed the donor, shall measure it with his hand and prepare the *kaṭhina* robe from it;
he should then present it to the donor, saying, "This is for you, O donor.
For the *kaṭhina* robe is of two kinds: that which has been made and that which has not been made.

In that regard, according to the classification of types, it is made either of three or five sections; in width it is no less than three cubits, and in length it is no less than five cubits. It may be well-sewn and manufactured, or unsewn and unmanufactured. Furthermore, each of these is of two kinds: finished and unfinished.
In that regard, the one upon which blue dots have been applied and which has been consecrated with the worship-mantra is "completed" (*niṣṭhita*);
the other is "uncompleted" (*aniṣṭhita*).
Here, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, [for] the donor...
The one who performs the ritual according to the rules, having taken the finished *kaṭhina* robe, should speak thus in the presence of the Noble Saṃgha that has resolved upon the three-month period:
"Venerable ones, please attend to me; with this robe, a donor named so-and-so will spread the *kaṭhina* in this monastic residence."
"May the noble Saṃgha dwell here; may the donor rejoice.
Having thus requested a second and a third time, the noble Saṃgha accepts that request.

Then, during the day, using ink-liquid or a blue dye-essence, one applies four drops on the edge for the purification of the Four Truths and so forth, or three for the purification of the Three Jewels and so forth, or two for the purification of the equipment for yoga and so forth.
One should perform this according to the prescribed rite.

When night has turned into dawn, at the designated time, [the site] should be prepared, strewn with divine and fragrant flowers, perfumes, and the like; with parasols, banners, and flags raised high; with small heaps of incense placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions; and with bright staff-lamps and incense burners set out.

In a suitable location— on a bed, a couch, or a broad seat— one should spread out and establish the hard robe (*kaṭhinacīvara*), which has been empowered by mantra and worshipped with the five offerings.

Thereafter, that faithful donor, having honored it with sublime offerings and prostrated before it, should give gold, silver, copper, and other metallic substances, as well as gems such as emerald, ruby, diamond,
lapis lazuli, sapphire, and so forth, along with divine garments and ornaments, to that hard robe for the sake of the Three Jewels.

One should write down on a leaf or similar surface the names of fields—such as gardens, houses, groves, and parks—as well as female and male slaves, elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, along with the income from grain and other sources; this constitutes "external wealth" (*bāhyadhana*), which one should bestow right there. Furthermore, there are various items fit for enjoyment, such as foods that are chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk; vessels and the five types of utensils; beds, seats, and so on; medicinal substances; and various other articles. This is "solid" (*kaṭhina*).
Having touched it, he should distribute it for the use of the Saṅgha from his side.
This is the *kaṭhina*.
Then, the venerable monk named Sumanas said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhagavān, for what reason is the robe and so forth called *kaṭhina*?
The Bhagavān replied, "Venerable one, that which is firm, pure, indestructible, and vast and imperishable is called *kaṭhina*."

For indeed, because of the firmness of the donor's intention, the purity of the robe, the indivisibility of the Saṅgha, and the vastness and indestructibility of the fruit of the gift, everything becomes meritorious.
Having wandered through the city of Śrāvastī, the Charioteer of Men,
having liberated his mind from the bondage of the snake, passed away.
With his senses stilled and his mind completely tranquil, the Jina invited his own disciples.

In the great city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the delightful park of Anāthapiṇḍada— perfumed with fragrant incense, adorned with heaps of sweet-smelling flowers, and situated in a pure precinct— the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord Śākyamuni, the Great Compassionate One who possesses pure awakening and has destroyed all faults, was dwelling together with a great assembly of followers upon a vast and precious throne. Then the Blessed One, remaining in silence, directed his worldly mind toward performing the tenfold activity of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.

Then, having recollected the evil deed committed against the Tathāgata when incited by the heretical wanderers, the elder monks were overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). With their hands joined in reverence upon their heads, they prostrated before the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One, who was seated upon a great throne, and addressed him as follows:
"The Blessed One has delivered many discourses concerning the Dharma, and many beings have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
"Furthermore, many other deeds of a Buddha have been performed by us as well: first, the thought of awakening was generated, and many perfectly enlightened Buddhas were attended upon.
What if we were to go to Lake Anavatapta and, in the presence of the Blessed One, each recount our own karmic history?
May the Blessed One grant his consent."
It is indeed the natural law (dharmatā) of the Blessed Buddhas—while they are living, staying, maintaining themselves, and carrying on—that there are ten necessary duties to be performed.
What are the ten? The Buddha-Bhagavats do not pass into final nirvana as long as they have not yet prophesied [the enlightenment of] a Buddha.
As long as the mind for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment has not been generated by many beings;
as long as all those to be trained have not been trained;
and as long as the pair of foremost disciples has not been designated.
As long as the boundary has not been established;
as long as the fifth portion of his life has not been relinquished;
and as long as the Great Miracle has not been displayed in the great city of Śrāvastī.
Until the descent of the gods has been manifested in the city of Śākāśya;
until my mother and father have been established in the truths;
and until the net of past karma has been explained before the great lake Anavatapta together with the community of disciples.
Then, having taken it to heart, the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, made a prophecy.
Desiring to explain the previous web of karma at Lake Anavatapta, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Having heard those spoken words and having received the command of the Great Seer, the disciples of the Sugata..."
Then those foremost of persons went by means of their supernatural power, just as swans follow the lord of swans in the sky.
Just as another [king] is surrounded by a flock of swans, so too was the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni;
like Garuḍa surrounded by birds with red wings, he emerged from the Jetavana monastery through the air, accompanied by nearly five hundred arhats who were emitting a manifold web of shimmering rays,
and together with four hundred and ninety-nine who were free from passion.

Then the Blessed One, together with the great community of śrāvakas, vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared at the Great Lake Anavatapta, situated to the north of Mount Mahākīṭa, which lies to the north of Mount Gandhamādana in the Himalayas. That lake is so called because no heat of the afflictions, such as passion and the like, exists within it.
That is the great lake Anavatapta;
it is forty-four yojanas on each side and forty yojanas deep.
This delightful place, frequented by fierce yakṣas, is beautifully adorned with trees bearing various flowers;
from here, four rivers carrying water flow toward the ocean, spreading out in the four directions.
Mortals do not cross the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Nadī, the Vakṣu, and the Śītā;
unless one has attained the power of supernatural success (*ṛddhi*), alas, I must go here to the great ocean lake.
It was beautifully adorned with various kinds of multicolored flowers and trees bearing sweet-smelling, delicious fruits; furthermore, it was filled with cool, pure, and delicious water,
and graced by blossoms such as the lotus, the blue water-lily, the white water-lily, the kahlāra, and the red lotus.

Furthermore, it was delightful with the warbling of various birds such as cranes, peacocks, ruddy geese, herons, egrets, ospreys, and curlews; moreover, it resounded with the songs and warblings of swarms of female bees greedy for drinking nectar;
and it was graced by hosts of gods, asuras, humans, kinnaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents, and apsarases.
Then, while residing there, the Blessed One gave rise to a worldly thought.

It is indeed the nature of things that at whatever time the Buddha-Blessed Ones give rise to a worldly thought, at that very moment even the smallest creatures, down to the ants and termites, perceive the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.

Then the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, perceived that the Blessed One, together with his community of disciples, desired to explain the sequence of past karma regarding this lake; having understood this through the Buddha’s supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), they created in the middle of the great lake a royal lotus surrounded by many other lotuses, measuring as much as a cartwheel, with a thousand petals, a shimmering jeweled stalk, diamond-hard filaments, and a blazing pericarp.

A golden lotus was fashioned for the sake of the Blessed One’s seat; then the Blessed One sat down upon its pericarp, and the monks also sat down upon the pericarps of other lotuses facing the Blessed One. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain sewing his outer robe (saṃghāṭī).
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and bring a companion for the going-forth.
"So be it, Blessed One," the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One, and having accepted his word, he vanished from the great lake Anavatapta.
He stayed on Vulture Peak Mountain and, in the presence of the venerable Śāriputra, spoke thus:

"O Śāriputra, the Teacher, together with four hundred and ninety-nine arhats, desires to explain his former karmic connections at the great lake Anavatapta; he remains waiting for you. Come, let us go."
Śāriputra said,
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I will first sew this outer robe (saṃghāṭī) and then I shall come.
Then Maudgalyāyana, unable to endure those words, used his supernatural power (ṛddhi) to bind five fingers onto him.
Even with such great supernatural power, he remained sewing it.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if that is so, let there be thread for the outer robe.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, if you will not go, then this outer robe (saṃghāṭī) must first be sewn;
after that, you may go.
Venerable Śāriputra, I shall provide assistance."
Śāriputra said, "Do so.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by means of his own supernatural power, began to sew it with five fingers.
He was addressed by the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if it is so, let it be another sūtra.
He replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, if you do not go after doing this,
I shall carry you away by the power of my supernatural faculties.
Then the venerable Śāriputra, having loosened his blindfold, said:

"For indeed, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you have been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers. Therefore, you shall surely lead me there by your strength.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana drew him along.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra reflected: "He possesses great supernatural power and great majesty; it is possible that he will summon [the other]."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra fixed Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana drew it along with Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
The Venerable Śāriputra thought, "He will even drag away Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa! The Venerable Śāriputra fixed his attention upon Sumeru, the king of mountains,
and it was dragged away by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
At that time, even Sumeru, the king of mountains, trembled;
at that time, even the two naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, were greatly agitated.
When they become thus agitated, the monks question the Buddha, the Blessed One.
“Blessed One, have the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda become agitated,
such that the great lake Anavatapta has been stirred up?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was not the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda who were agitated;
rather, it was a great display of supernatural power performed by the two great śrāvakas against one another.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra reflected:"
Thinking, "He will even draw forth Sumeru,
the king of mountains," he then fastened the lotus stalk to that very lotus pericarp upon which the Blessed One was seated;
thereupon, it remained perfectly motionless.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"You have performed a great display of supernatural power;
very well, come, let us go."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said,
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I too shall come alone until the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrives.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra went first, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down upon the pericarp of his own lotus-seat.
Thereafter, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrived and took his place on his own seat. He was addressed by him:
"Venerable Śāriputra, have you come?"
He said, "I have come. Then all the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Behold, venerable sir, how the Blessed One has declared the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana to be of great psychic power and great majesty, the foremost among those possessed of psychic powers."
He too was defeated by the venerable Śāriputra through supernatural power.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he was defeated by him through this very craft."
Listen to that for a moment.
Once upon a time, monks, there was a master painter in the Middle Country.
On account of some business, he went to the realm of the Yavanas and stayed at the residence of a master mechanic; having performed his meals and other duties there, he settled down.
Therefore, having fashioned for him a wooden mechanical doll, he sent it as an attendant and companion.
That wooden mechanical doll stood there holding an oil-ointment in its hand.
Then she was addressed by him:
"Come here!
She remained silent.
He reflected, "Surely a female attendant has been sent to wait upon me."
She was described:
"Aha! By the Creator, this woman has been fashioned as if from the essence of jewels.
By her, the merit of my eyes has been purified."
"Shame! Woe to that man born in Jambudvīpa who does not have such a young woman—endowed with beauty and youth, most enchanting—within reach of his eye, his hand, or the touch of her body!
Having been thus honored with these nectar-like, sweet words, he began to summon her, saying:
"My dear Sundarī, come, come here!"
Nevertheless, concluding that the wooden mechanical doll had not said anything at all, he approached her in haste with a mind obsessed by desire.
Having seized her with his hand and pulled her, she then stood there as a heap of wooden joints;
thus, he was made an object of derisive laughter.
He reflected:
"I have been betrayed by him while alone;
I too shall do the same."
Thinking, "Lest he fall into ridicule and exposure in the midst of this assembly including the king," he painted himself with a garland of thorns hanging from his neck facing the door;
immediately thereafter, he remained hidden behind the surface of the door-panel,
having passed the time until the moment of his [the king's] departure.
That master mechanic reflected:
"The sun has set;
for what reason does he not bring it out?"
He went there and saw him;
having seen him, he reflected:
"What is the reason he has hanged himself?
As soon as he looked, he saw a heap of wooden beams and perceived that he had hanged himself by means of a split beam.
It is the custom here in the Yavana territory that if anyone dies in another world while a guest in someone's house,
the funeral rites for him are not performed until it has been reported to the king.
The king was informed by him:

"Your Majesty, a master painter has arrived here from the Middle Country. He has taken up residence in my quarters, and I sent a female attendant to him after having fashioned for him a mechanical wooden puppet.
She was seized by his hand and delighted; at that moment, a heap of wooden joints remained standing."
"Therefore, Pratibhinnaka has hanged himself.
Your Majesty, please examine him; afterwards, I shall perform the funeral rites.
By the king's command, the ministers went there.
He was seen by them;
having seen him, they said,
"How is he to be lowered down from our ivory peg?"
Others said,
"The snare must be cut.
Thereupon, he took an axe and began to cut the snare.
When that master mechanic had been cut down and lay there with his head split open,
he emerged from between the door-panels and said:
"O man, I have been struck down by you alone!"
"But you, on the other hand, have been exposed by me in the midst of the assembly including the king.
What do you think, monks?
That master painter was none other than this monk Śāriputra.
That very master of mechanical arts was this monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
even then he was defeated by him through that very craft,
and now as well, he has been defeated by him.
Furthermore, hear how he was defeated by him.
Once upon a time, monks,
a dispute arose between two master painters.
One said,
"I know a beautiful craft. The other said, "So do I."
"I possess excellent craftsmanship.

Then, out of this dispute, they both approached the king; having approached him, they spoke in the presence of the king: "I possess excellent craftsmanship," and the other also said, "I too possess excellent craftsmanship."
Then the king pointed out the courtyard at the gate, saying,
"Gentlemen, I do not know which of you knows your craft;
however, let one of you polish a single wall."

The second one also did the same for the other wall; having placed a curtain between them, the two began to paint. One completed the work of painting in six months, while the second also completed the preparation of the wall in six months.
The one who had performed the painting work approached the king;
having approached him, he said,
"Your Majesty, my painting work is completed."
"O Great King, look!
The king has gone out accompanied by his minister.
Then it was seen by the king.
Upon seeing this, he said, "This painting is beautiful.
The second one also said, "Your Majesty, please look at the work of art;
the shadow has fallen upon it."
Seeing that, the king said, "This painting work is exceedingly clear.
He too, drawing aside the curtain, said,
"This is not painting work."
Rather, it was the plastering of the wall. Thus the king was filled with wonder and addressed his ministers.
"Gentlemen, this artisan is most excellent.
What do you think, monks,
regarding him who completed the plastering of the wall in six months?
"This very person is that monk Śāriputra,
by whom the painting was executed in six months;
this very person is that monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who even then was surpassed by him in craftsmanship."
"Even now he has been defeated by means of this supernatural power.
Furthermore, he was defeated by supernatural power once again;
listen to that.
In ancient times, there were two sages named Śaṅkha and Likhita in Vārāṇasī.
A dispute arose between them over the matter of rain and drought.
Then, on one occasion, the matted-haired sage was touched by Śaṅkha with his feet, and he became enraged.
Likhita said to him, "May your head split asunder at sunrise!
Śaṅkha replied, "By my word, the sun shall not rise.
When he had spoken thus, the world remained in deep darkness for a very long time.
Out of compassion, he fashioned for him a head out of clay and drew it;
then, at sunrise, that head suddenly shattered into a hundred pieces upon the earth.
That Śaṅkha, having been born in another life, has today attained the state of Maudgalyāyana.

This Śāriputra was written down [as a scribe], yet even then he was the victor; likewise, even now he has been defeated by his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), and so on—this should be understood in detail. Of those meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) which the Tathāgata possesses, the Pratyekabuddhas do not know even their names.
Of those [attainments] for which the Pratyekabuddhas are recipients, Śāriputra does not even know their names;
of those for which Śāriputra is a recipient, Maudgalyāyana does not even know their names;
and of those for which Maudgalyāyana is a recipient, the other Śrāvakas do not even know their names.

Therefore, although this Śāriputra possesses great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), he was designated by me as the foremost among those possessing supernatural powers with reference to those who dwell frequently [in meditation].
Immediately following this, he said: "Having gone there, he should utter these words."
He who remembers his former abodes and recounts there the conduct consistent with them,
he shall know the auspicious and inauspicious karma that results in the arising of happiness.
Then the elder monks, by the command of the Tathāgata, each recounted their own web of karma.
First of all, the monk Nāgila, possessed of great eloquence, spoke:
"The monk named Nāgila was a disciple of the Buddha."
Being asked a question, he gave an explanation at the great lake, the Anavatapta Saras.
Then a monk named Nāgila, having joined his ten fingers in reverential salutation before the Tathāgata, declared his own web of karma:
"Having given the *kaṭhina* robe to the Saṃgha with a mind of perfect clarity..."
For thirty great eons from now, I do not recall falling into an evil rebirth;
for eighteen eons...
I delight in the world of the gods;
indeed, sixty-four times have I exercised the sovereignty of the lord of the gods.
I have become a universal monarch one hundred and eighty times,
as well as a regional king.
No number of them exists for me.
Aho! Wherever human beings perform service to the Three Jewels, [there I am].
Having given even a small amount,
they obtain a vast fruit— if my birth is among mortals. || 4 ||
Having abandoned great divine happiness,
I am honored by mortals; that is the fruit of my harsh austerities.
If there were to be rebirth as a god,
having abandoned human happiness,
I would be worthy of worship by the host of gods.
That is the fruit of the gift of the *kaṭhina*:
[the earth] up to the Cakravāḍa mountains, including the oceans and the continents.
"Even while desiring it,
I cover myself with impurities as if with a garment.
Furthermore, speaking of the excellence of even a harsh gift, he says:
With every step I take, my enemies appear before me;
yet I stand upon those very enemies.
Even the canopy has been defiled;
the doors have been opened for me,
and the afflictions have been mastered by me.
All outflows are completely exhausted;
that is the fruit of the gift of the hard [seat].
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are—
The eight liberations as well, and the six supernormal powers have been attained; the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled. 10
With a fragrant body, he goes to the world of the gods; possessing great wealth, he is the master of enjoyments and happiness,
and the scent of his pure conduct wafts through all directions.
Indeed, through the offering of fragrance, one proceeds toward liberation.
Those endowed with faith who offer fragrant flowers to the Sugata in the assembly of the Saṅgha will shine like flowers; they shall follow the path to heaven and attain liberation for all the world.
Those endowed with the fragrance of true ethical discipline are incessantly honored by gods and asuras alike;
from their bodies the most excellent scent emanates, they become happy, and their faculty of smell is purified.
One should cause a dense and variegated garland to be offered to the assembly of deities;
then the pain in the head is not felt, and one becomes a traveler through the sky. Those who offer flowers and incense with sincere devotion to the assembly of the Enemy of Manmatha [Śiva]—
Those who practice *śīla* always attain happiness; being joyful, they become lords of enjoyments.
Their mindfulness does not falter; being self-controlled, they have found their footing in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
These captivating ones of sharp intellect attain peace; they are worthy of worship by gods and asuras alike. (Incense)
He possesses eyes that are delightful to behold, with large blue eyes; his treasury is well-filled, and he is one to be gazed upon by both men and women.
Whoever offers a garland of lamps to the Saṅgha will possess radiant complexions, soft and delicate feet,
and great strength, remaining invincible to their enemies.
By the gift of oil, mortals become beautiful in form and attain happiness;
one who gives a pair of leather sandals with a joyful mind [attains the same].
He will be a possessor of supernatural powers and rich in wealth;
that great-souled one, with well-proportioned feet,
will traverse the heavens, traveling in an excellent vehicle.
As soon as that Sage was born, he took seven steps with powerful strides upon the earth;
a row of lotuses was formed [at each step], which indeed became the fruit [of his birth].
How could she have obtained that pair of sandals otherwise?
By the gift of an umbrella, he becomes a protector from the heat for the worlds;
by the gift of shade, he dwells for a very long time in the delightful shade of royal fortune with ease.
He becomes the master of the Dharma and certainly the protector of the entire world; endowed with beauty and obtaining enjoyments, he shall not go to the dense thicket of evil destinies.
Having first joyfully raised the parasol over the womb of the earth-element of Kāśyapa in the past,
that Great-Souled One enjoyed happiness both in heaven and on earth.

The great-souled Nanda attained tranquility. By the gift of a needle for thread, one certainly becomes a possessor of wisdom; through the attainment of wisdom, that treasury of intelligence is liberated from the fears of the states of existence.

Wisdom is the queen in the removal of misfortune; there is no other like it. One who is endowed with it becomes successful in every way through that very attainment. [One should fashion] a needle for the thread, resembling pure crystal, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length.
He who gives chalk here is born as a great scholar. One who gives chalk becomes endowed with enjoyments, possesses a captivating and fragrant countenance,
and is freed from diseases such as excessive phlegm, possessing a pleasing voice.
Free from mental afflictions, he partakes of birth among the gods;
his conduct is marked by the budding grace of offering betel-leaf.
With a face adorned with auspicious marks, he is delightful to the eyes.
With copper-red lips and a row of beautiful, tender teeth, and lovely cheeks free from the afflictions of phlegm and worms—this is the foremost fruit brought about by the gift of betel. 2. Betel.
Whether in heaven or on earth, there is no other way to adorn the body— whether it be the neck, head, feet, or arms— with ornaments made of beryl and gold, together with pearls.
Therefore, they declare clothing to be the most excellent ornament.
Even one endowed with beauty, born of noble lineage, wise, and having exerted effort in many scriptural traditions—
For even a man who is fully adorned with a multitude of virtues such as moral conduct does not truly shine on this earth without clothing;
therefore, one should regard clothing as an incomparable ornament.
It wards off cold, heat, gadflies, and mosquitoes; it is an incomparable garment of modesty. Therefore, by men who have attained their desires, the gift of clothing should be given repeatedly. 3.
Seated upon a lion throne with golden fly-whisks shimmering like moonbeams and white parasols held aloft,
though his head was adorned with crowns of gold and jewels, he remained as before.
Even a glorious universal monarch does not shine without clothing.
[4] In the cities of Alakā where the illustrious Lord of Wealth dwells,
and in Bhogavatī adorned with jewels upon thousands of tongues;
Even Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra do not shine without garments amidst the assembly of gods on the peaks of Kailāsa and Meru; yet,
having given [a garment] variegated with beautiful tawny [threads], fashioned with clusters of flowers, and dyed in blue, yellow, and white—
With red and other beautiful, most radiant garments and fine robes, and wearing lovely garlands and divine,
exquisite clothes, that son of the Sugata— handsome, charming,
his self adorned with the garment of modesty, and possessed of keen intelligence— becomes a lord of all dharmas. (Garment)
Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, numerous bracelets, armlets, and various kinds of earrings,
mortals move about as disciples of the Sugata.
Having bestowed various ornaments,
fire, poison, weapons, and even a rain of thunderbolts do not affect his body.
By the gift of copper and other materials to the Jina’s Saṅgha, a mortal dwells in loving-kindness.

Wherever a person is born, they become worthy of worship and salutation with vessels of copper and other metals; having attained heaven, they possess vast wealth and are highly esteemed in the assemblies of the virtuous.

One born into a high, illustrious, and very great family becomes devoted to enjoyments; yet, by giving a seat, one possessing incomparable virtues shall attain peace. Through the power of the seat, one becomes a king endowed with a stable position and great supernatural majesty.
By giving food to the Saṅgha, one prospers in happiness everywhere; born from such a gift of food, one will be reborn in a noble family, possessed of good character,
worthy of being served by men, and beautiful to behold.
He became gracious, wise, happy, golden-hued,
and glorious through the offering of *śāli* rice; by offering the sacrificial ladle,
*laḍḍuka*, *pūraka*, and *paulikā* cakes.
By offering various cakes, *karambha*, and *parpaṭa*,
along with *satakraka* (sour gruel) to the excellent Gaṇa, one becomes a lord devoted to enjoyment; [as do those who offer] *laḍḍuka* and other sweets.
Those men who, having placed curd, soma, clarified butter, honey, sugar, and molasses into vessels made of gold, silver, and other materials, offer them to the Gaṇas;

The five kinds of nectar-eaters, endowed with power, having filled a jar with the water of the five essences and offered it to the supreme Gaṇa, enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure and sever eternal craving. The jar—
By the gift of a water-pot and an alms-bowl, one becomes endowed with the knowledge of the Dharma and is born equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) within the Three Jewels.
By giving a house to the supreme Gaṇa, one becomes a possessor of a water-pot and a vessel who gives everything;
indeed, with all desires fulfilled, he prospers in happiness everywhere. House.
By that very gift of the wish-fulfilling tree, he shall become complete;
he will become a human being in Uttarakuru, possessing great enjoyments.
The great merit of giving a wish-fulfilling tree bell is that one becomes handsome and always possesses a joyful mind.

He becomes one whose voice is pleasing to gods and asuras, and who resembles the king of the gandharvas. He who, with a serene intention, gives bells to the Saṅgha and various medicinal provisions, is not touched by the sufferings arising from the occurrence of the intermediate kalpa of disease.
Freed from disease, old age, and the like, he lives happily with undivided resolve; for, being devoid of the diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he attains ultimate health.
In a previous life, having set out as a physician, he was turned away by one clad in bark garments.
There, in that untroubled community, he requested medicine.
Out of compassion and a desire to favor him, a certain person free from passion [provided it].
Having eaten a single *harītakī* fruit, he accomplished that deed.
For five hundred births, not even the slightest illness occurred to him.
Having abandoned the disease of affliction (*kleśa*), he attained liberation in his final existence. [This is] the medicine.
He who offers here to the stainless Saṅgha water that is clear, free from odor, very light, endowed with a pleasant taste, and cool—
being himself free from the heat of affliction through pure body, speech, and mind— he is happy like one who has drawn his sword.
He destroys craving; he does not merely abandon it, but abandons even the craving for cyclic existence.
In the teaching of Kāśyapa, the monk Yaśomitra served water to the community for twelve thousand years.
By the ripening of that karma, for five hundred births, he—

He did not experience even in dreams the suffering caused by thirst. Those who joyfully offer water to the assembly— beverages that sever craving, which are heart-pleasing, endowed with delicious flavors, possessing a potent taste, and delightful with their fragrance— [attain this state].

Having cut with wisdom the creeper of craving that arises from the passion for existence, they cross to the further shore of the ocean of becoming; having given the auspicious drink, they certainly reach the end of the sea of existence. [They attain] a drink for those of immeasurable wealth, accompanied by horses and elephants.

Having reached land surrounded by the ocean, a king who possesses great splendor and beauty among men becomes even more radiant through the gift of land, surpassing the palaces of kings who have vast retinues. Land.
Whoever, endowed with faith, bestows various grains, fruits, and so forth upon the Saṅgha,
for that person the desired fruit ripens eternally.
Every fruit ripens on the path to enlightenment.
Merit is the rice for men; it is a lamp in the darkness, a protection in times of fear, and a kinsman in times of calamity.
It is the unsurpassed medicine for ailments and the boat across the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Wealth comes through giving, not from harming others; heaven through ethical conduct, not by leaping from mountain precipices;
purity through truthfulness, not by entering water.
Liberation comes through knowledge, not from the emaciation of the body.
Through the taking of what is not given, one becomes poor;
and because of poverty, one commits evil deeds.
Having committed evil, one goes to hell.
Though liberated from hell, the sinner is once again [bound].
Generosity destroys poverty; ethical discipline destroys rebirth in the lower realms;
wisdom destroys ignorance; and meditative cultivation destroys cyclic existence.
When a person gives their own wealth with a pure mind,
that very moment the accumulation of merit is designated as "giving."
May Lakṣmī, ever blazing, dwell here; may Fame, ever radiant, also abide; may the sovereign, having utterly destroyed his enemies, protect the earth for a long time, free from disease and famine;

may those worthy of offerings, rich in virtuous conduct, constantly attain growth within the collection of the teachings; and may the unshakable dispensation of the Blessed One triumph, as bright as the moon and sun until the end of time.
May the lord of the earth rule the world according to the Dharma;
may people be devoted to the worship of the Three Jewels; and may families have abundant herds of cattle and be free from all evils.
And may the subjects, possessing excellent progeny, always rejoice.
The sun shines in the sky as long as the moon, with its orb wreathed in rays and marked by the deer,
has not risen; and the lotus-dwellers sport unimpededly in their own domain for as long as [the moon remains].
May the teaching of the Sugata, which is honored by gods and asuras, endure.
Then the elder monks questioned the Blessed One:
"What karma was performed by the Blessed One?"
"By the ripening of which karma was the big toe of the Blessed One wounded by a stone fragment when he had attained full enlightenment?
The Blessed One said,
"Monks, these actions were performed by the Tathāgata himself," and so on in detail.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Long ago, monks, in a past age, innumerable eons ago, there lived a householder in a certain mountain village.
He brought home a wife who was his equal.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.
While he was playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, a son was born.
He was raised and grew until he became a great man.
Then, at another time, the wife of that householder passed away.
He took another wife, and while he was sporting, enjoying himself, and amusing himself with her, a son was born to him.
He then provided a residence for his eldest son.
While the son was playing, enjoying himself, and amusing himself, a son was born to him and a daughter was also born.
Then, at a later time, the householder passed away along with his wife.
That boy remained in the presence of his own brother.
That householder’s son was addressed by his wife:
"Noble sir, this boy belongs to you."
"This man is my brother.
She said,
"Noble son, a share of the house must also be given to him."
He said,
"Half belongs to you, and half belongs to us.
She said:
"Noble son, having become the share of this one man alone, half shall belong to us who are many.
He replied,
"This is the way of the world."
She said, "Noble son, if it is so, then have him killed.
He replied, "My dear lady, how indeed could I kill my own brother for the sake of wealth?"
She said to him again and again,
"For one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is indeed no evil deed that should not be committed.
He consented to this.
He said to his brother:
"Brother, let us go to the forest for the sake of obtaining flowers."
He went with him;
there, having cast him into a mountain cave, he struck him down with a stone. What do you think, monks?
That householder’s son who,
for the sake of his own wealth, had that half-brother killed—
was none other than I at that time and on that occasion.
Because I had previously killed my half-brother for the sake of his wealth,
as the ripening of that karma, I was reborn in the hells for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years.
By the remaining residue of that very same karma, my foot is now wounded by a pebble while the Tathāgata has attained perfect awakening.
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the ripening of which resulted in his foot being wounded by a thorn of *khadira* wood when he had attained full enlightenment?
"Monks, these actions were performed by the Tathāgata himself," [the Buddha said], and so on in detail.
"In the past, monks, there were two caravan leaders who, having skillfully prepared a sea-going vessel, set out upon the great ocean to gather wealth."
Then, by a favorable wind, they reached the Island of Jewels; there,
one [of them] filled a ship with a cargo of jewels,
and the second with a cargo of women.
The two set out. There, the boat belonging to the one who had filled it beyond its capacity met with disaster.
Having weighed [the goods] with that caravan leader using a scale and removed the jewels, he addressed the caravan leader.
He reflected:
"This man will go away having achieved his purpose, while I shall go away having failed in my purpose."
He began to pierce that vessel. While it was being pierced, he was seen by the caravan leader, who said, "Do not pierce the vessel!"
"Lest we all fall into calamity through such misconduct.
Though he was thus restrained, he did not desist;
he was killed by that blow from the spear.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that caravan leader, by whom [I] was struck down with a blow of a spear—
at that time, on that occasion, I myself was the one struck down by him with a blow of a spear.
As the ripening of that karma, he was reborn in the hells for many hundreds of years, many millions, billions, and trillions of years.
By the remainder of that very same karma, the foot of the Tathāgata, once he had attained full awakening, was wounded by a thorn from a *khadira* tree.
“Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the ripening of which resulted in his being falsely accused by the young woman Sundarī?
“Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself,” and so on in detail, up to: “Indeed, for embodied beings, [karma] surely bears fruit.”
In the past, monks, in a time long gone,
when the lifespan of beings was eighty thousand years, a teacher named Vipaśyin appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, a Blessed One.
Under the teaching of the Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, two brothers, Vasiṣṭha and Bharadvāja, went forth into homelessness.
Vasiṣṭha realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Bharadvāja, while reciting and studying, mastered the three baskets;
he became a master of the Tripiṭaka.
He possessed eloquence that was both appropriate and unrestrained.
By him, the householder was converted;
for his sake, he caused a monastery to be built, fully equipped with all necessary requisites.
"Therefore, let us go and take up residence together with that brother of his.
He went there and was seen by that householder.
Seeing that the monk was an Arhat, serene in body and serene in mind, he became filled with faith.
Having honored him with that [offering] born of faith, he covered him with a costly garment.
He was seen by his brother, who thought:
"I have always been the one who goes before this householder in all matters."

He covered it with a cloth, thinking, "It is covered," and became intent on bringing it down in his presence. He saw him standing there agitated and reflected, "If I give this to him, he will enter into a state of even greater faith. Having thought this, he bestowed it upon him.
"Let it be yours alone.
A servant girl belonging to that householder came to that monastery and performed the maintenance work;
she was addressed by him as follows:
"Daughter, I give this pair of garments to you.
You must do as I say.
She replied:
"Noble sir, what should I do?
You should put on that pair of garments and perform the household chores.
If the mistress of the house asks, 'Whence did you get this pair of garments?', you should say, 'It was given to me by such-and-such a noble man.'"
If he asks, "For whose sake was this given to you by my noble brother? one should say, "My noble brother should also be asked: for what purpose do men bestow gifts upon courtesans?
She, having put on that garment, began to perform the household chores.
He was recognized by that householder.
He said to her,
"Girl, where did you get this pair of garments?"
She said, "This was given to me by this noble man. [The other asked:
"Girl, for what reason did this noble man bestow this pair of garments upon you?"
She said,
"Noble one, this too should be asked:
for what reason do men bestow [gifts] upon women?"
He began to manifest his lack of faith toward him;
for those great-souled ones are fearful of disrespect.
He rose and departed.
What do you think, monks?

He who was named Bharadvāja, by whom I was falsely accused when I was not yet an Arhat—was he anyone else at that time, on that occasion? It was I myself who, at that time and on that occasion, was falsely accused as an Arhat monk by him when I was not one.
As the ripening of that karma, he was reborn in the hells for many hundreds of thousands of years and many hundreds of millions of years;
until now, by the remainder of that very same karma, the Tathāgata has been falsely accused by the young woman Sundarikā, and so forth, as detailed at length.
